before: Midnight. My office was a room over a tailor’s on Mulberry Street, with my name on the door in gold leaf that was coming off one letter at a time. The coffee I’d made was cold by the time I remembered it. I drank it anyway; it was lighter than holding my head. ¶
after: ¶ “Somebody has taken my Pomeranian,” Schilling said. “Duchess. Gone from her cushion by the radiator, just like that.”
target: Somebody knocked twice, politely, and then a third time, less politely. My visitor knocked once, came in, and sat down like somebody who’d been rehearsing it on the stairs.

before: From there to the Schilling flat was a good walk. There were lace mats on every chair back and photographs on every wall, looking down at me as if I’d come in with my boots on. A china shepherdess stood on a doily, looking at the room with painted patience. ¶
after: ¶ Nobody in the place was paid to notice who came and went, so nobody had.
target: Schilling had left everything just as it was, so that Duchess would know the way home.

before: I went over the parlor, and then the door, and then the parlor again. ¶ Schilling kept out of my way, the way people keep out of the way of a doctor. ¶ The cushion by the radiator was empty. There wasn’t a mark on the door or the window. Whoever came in had a key. ¶
after: ¶ Alfano could tell me her own evening, and she was at the chop house.
target: So the key that let them in was the spare, and the spare lived on the nail in the hall at the Delmonico rooms.

before: I walked it at an ordinary pace, downtown and west to the Delmonico rooms, a couple of blocks, and wrote it down. An hour only holds so many walks like that. The dance hall crowd would have finished saying goodnight by now. It had taken them long enough, but they’d done it properly. ¶ The Delmonico rooms over the fish market were up a steep stair from Catherine Street, three floors of them. The market below was shut and its stalls hosed down, but the smell of fish hadn’t gone anywhere. She had a big ring of keys at her waist and reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and looked at my shoes before my face, to see what they’d do to the stairs. Bernstein was in the front room with a book, one finger in it to keep the place. ¶ The spare key lived on the nail in the hall here. That settled where I was going. ¶
after: ¶ A clock in the hall was keeping time for nobody in particular.
target: A landlady who sits on her stairs knows who used them.

before: I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Mrs. Callahan. ¶ I waited for a gap in her night, and when one came I stepped into it. I asked Mrs. Callahan to take me through the night, hour by hour, everybody in the place. ¶ She looked at the door, as if the night were written on it, and started. ¶ “Eight o’clock, Alfano, Bernstein and Doyle. Nobody else. Nine, Margolis, Bernstein and Doyle. Nobody else at all. Ten, Bernstein and Doyle. Nobody else, that hour. The spare key for the Schilling flat was on its nail at eight. I didn’t look again.” ¶ That put Bernstein here at ten, by her count. ¶
after: ¶ Alfano hadn’t told me her evening yet, and she was at the chop house.
target: It turned out Doyle was in the front room, in the good chair.

before: The chop house was a couple of blocks uptown, and I took it at a good clip. The street was empty and clear and very quiet, and my heels were the loudest thing on it. ¶ The Grand Street chop house had served steaks to three generations of men whose doctors had told them to stop. The doctors were right, and so were the steaks. A big samovar sat at the end of the counter, steaming quietly to itself. ¶ Mulcahy stood by the reservation book at the door with a pencil, crossing out tables nobody would want now. Margolis sat with her coat on and her plate pushed away, finishing a glass of seltzer. She smelled of gasoline and cold coffee and kept her gloves on indoors, the fingertips cut out of them. Alfano had a table by the window and a glass of tea gone cold. ¶
after: ¶ I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.
target: Nobody sits down in a restaurant without the head waiter deciding where, and Mulcahy had been doing the deciding.

before: I took the chair opposite Alfano and kept my hands where she could see them, on the tablecloth. ¶ “Mrs. Callahan has you at the Delmonico rooms at eight. Fill in the rest of the evening for me, in order.” She put down what she was holding and gave me her attention. ¶ “I was home at the Delmonico rooms at eight, with Bernstein and Doyle. Then at nine I went to the chop house for coffee and pie, with Shapiro. Come ten, I turned in early, home at the Delmonico rooms, on my own.” ¶ Alfano said home at ten. Mrs. Callahan had Bernstein and Doyle at the Delmonico rooms at ten o’clock, and nobody else. One of them was wrong. ¶ It turned out Shapiro was at a table by the wall, behind a menu. ¶ The samovar went on steaming at the end of the counter, the only thing in the room in no hurry at all. ¶ I went over it once more, the way you go over a bill you know is wrong. ¶
after: ¶ I could put it to Alfano now. Or I could find out first who Mulcahy had seen at the chop house.
target: Here’s what I had. She went at ten o’clock. Alfano had told me home at ten, and Mrs. Callahan’s list said otherwise. Bernstein was at the Delmonico rooms at ten; Mrs. Callahan said so. Margolis hadn’t told me where she was at ten, and nobody else had either.

before: Alfano had said she was here at nine. The head waiter sees everybody and says nothing, unless somebody asks. I was going to ask. I asked Mulcahy for a minute, and she gave me one, and kept an eye on the room the whole of it. ¶ I asked her to give me the night the way only the head waiter could: every face, every hour. She counted it off on her fingers, and ran out of fingers before she ran out of night. ¶ “Lou the bookmaker was in his back booth all evening, every hour of it. Eight o’clock, Margolis and Shapiro. Nobody else. Nine, Alfano and Shapiro. Nobody else at all. Ten, Margolis and Shapiro. Nobody else, that hour. after: ¶ “Something alive. It moved about.”
target: “What was it?” I said. “Under the coat.”

before: I found a chair at the chop house and sat down with the form. Every line on it had something under it now, and I knew whose word each one stood on. ¶
after: ¶ The coffee on my desk would have gone the rest of the way cold by now. I’d finish it anyway. I’d started it, and I’m a professional.
target: At ten Margolis was here, and Mulcahy said so. Bernstein was at the Delmonico rooms, and Mrs. Callahan said so. That left one person who could have had the spare key, with no true account for ten.

before: Midnight. My office was a room over a tailor’s on Mulberry Street, with my name on the door in gold leaf that was coming off one letter at a time. My ribs hurt when I breathed deep, so I breathed shallow. Rain ran down the window in the lamplight, and I sat and listened to it and did not move much. ¶ Somebody came up the stairs. Nobody comes up those stairs after midnight with good news; the good news waits for morning, like a gentleman. My visitor wiped his boots on the mat from habit, not respect. Nobody respects my floor. ¶ “It’s Mimi,” Hargrove said. “My Persian. She’s gone from the window seat.” ¶ I offered him the chair. He sat on the front half of it, which is the half I keep for clients. ¶ “I sat in the Velvet Room from eight until ten,” he said, “telling anybody who’d listen that I was off to my sister’s for the night, and the key was under the mat.” ¶ “And when did Mimi go missing?” ¶ “I can tell you when, near enough,” he said. “Whoever it was knocked the parlor clock off the shelf, and it stopped at ten past ten.” ¶ “Anybody you can think of who’d want Mimi?” ¶ “I keep thinking about Havemeyer,” Hargrove said. “She stood at my elbow at the Velvet Room the whole time, and I didn’t think anything of it at the time. And she is three weeks behind on the rent, and has been heard to say what a Persian with papers fetches.” ¶ He hesitated, then went on. “Doyle, a switchboard operator, lost her job on Friday, and asked me what Mimi was worth. And Pickering, a sewing-machine operator, owes Lou the bookmaker forty dollars, and Lou takes things in kind.” ¶
after: ¶ I took the money, and the night along with it.
target: He put ten dollars on the desk and smoothed it flat with his palm. “Find out who, and where.”

before: From there to the Hargrove flat was a good walk. A dance hall upstairs was letting out, and the street was full of people saying goodnight at length. ¶ I went up to the Hargrove flat on the third floor of 40 Avenue B. The stair carpet was worn to the threads in the middle, and the door at the top had a brass knocker that somebody polished every Saturday whether it needed it or not. A framed sampler on the wall said Bless This House in red cross-stitch. ¶ Hargrove had left everything just as it was, so that Mimi would know the way home. ¶
after: ¶ If she went at ten, the flat had been empty, and anybody who’d heard Hargrove at the Velvet Room had known the way in. That was a room, more or less. It was a big room.
target: Nobody in the place was paid to notice who came and went, so nobody had.

before: I went over Hargrove’s parlor from the door to the far wall, slowly. ¶ Hargrove sat on the arm of a chair and watched me go over his own parlor like a stranger’s. ¶ The window seat was empty but for white hairs. The key was back under the mat, and there wasn’t a mark on the door. Whoever it was had known exactly where to look. ¶ So it was somebody who’d heard Hargrove at the Velvet Room between eight and ten, and had come here after. That made the Velvet Room the place to start counting. ¶
after: ¶ The sampler went on blessing the house in red cross-stitch, whatever the house was up to.
target: The one to ask was the bartender at the Velvet Room, who’d been there all night.

before: It was a fair few blocks to the Velvet Room, west. I made a note of it: tonight was going to be about who could walk where in an hour. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶
after: ¶ Quill was polishing a glass that was already clean, which is what bartenders do instead of watching you. He had a pleasant, forgettable face, which in that trade is the whole trick, and eyes that went to the door every time it opened, and came back. Pickering was standing at the bar with her coat over her arm, drinking something brown in small careful sips.
target: I went down to the Velvet Room, six steps down under a hat shop. Upstairs the hat shop had gone dark, and down here the lamps were low and the talk was lower, the way it gets after midnight when the loud things have all been said. Behind the bar a moose head with one glass eye looked out over the bottles, having seen it all and liked none of it.

before: I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Quill. ¶ I waited for a gap in his night, and when one came I stepped into it. I asked him to count the night for me, face by face. ¶
after: ¶ “Lou the bookmaker was in his back booth all evening, every hour of it. Eight o’clock, Havemeyer, Pickering and Mr. Hargrove telling the room about his key. Nobody else. Nine, Havemeyer and Mr. Hargrove, still telling it. Nobody else at all. Ten, just Lou. Eleven: somebody came in with something under a coat and went straight to Lou, and it changed hands. I was watching the coat, not the face.”
target: He answered at once. It was all there, the way it always is with somebody whose job is to notice.

before: Quill’s list had Pickering here at eight. I wanted the rest of it in her own words. I leaned on the bar next to her and ordered nothing, which got noticed. Thin, and bent at the shoulders from years over a sewing machine, she wore clothes too good to have been bought. She’d made every stitch. ¶ I asked her to walk me through her night, every stop of it. ¶ She gave it to me in as few words as the evening would go into. ¶ “I was at the Velvet Room at eight, with Havemeyer. Nine o’clock I went up to Kowalski’s to see about some money owed, with Colquitt. Then at ten I went to the Velvet Room to settle a bet, on my own.” ¶ Pickering said the Velvet Room at ten. Quill had Lou here at ten o’clock, and nobody else. One of them was wrong. ¶ I buttoned my coat. It came off a rack, and in that company it knew it. ¶ I went over it once more, the way you go over a bill you know is wrong. ¶
after: ¶ I could put it to Pickering now. Or I could find out first from the landlady at Kowalski’s who’d been in.
target: Here’s what I had. She went at ten o’clock. Havemeyer and Pickering were at the Velvet Room while Hargrove told the room. Pickering had told me the Velvet Room at ten, and Quill’s list said otherwise. Havemeyer hadn’t told me where she was at ten, and nobody else had either. And whatever it was had gone to Lou at the Velvet Room at eleven.

before: Kowalski’s lay a couple of blocks east. A policeman on his round tried a shop door, found it locked, and looked almost disappointed. ¶ I went to Mrs. Kowalski’s boarding house on Orchard Street. It was a narrow brick house with a scrubbed stoop and a smell of beet soup that had got into the walls and settled. The stair had a brass rod on every step, and one of them was loose. ¶ Mrs. Kowalski was in the hall with a dustpan, sweeping a stair that had been swept already. She had a big ring of keys at her waist and reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and looked at my shoes before my face, to see what they’d do to the stairs. Havemeyer answered the door in her stocking feet, with the lamp behind her. Colquitt was still up, with the look of somebody who had been about to go to bed for an hour. ¶ Pickering had said she was here at nine, and that Havemeyer was with her at the Velvet Room at eight. That was reason enough. ¶
after: ¶ I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.
target: Nobody comes or goes in a rooming house without the landlady knowing, and Mrs. Kowalski had the look of a landlady who made a point of it.

before: Mrs. Kowalski met me at the foot of the stairs, which is where she met everybody. I asked her for everybody she’d seen tonight, in order, and nobody left out because she liked them. ¶ She looked at the door, as if the night were written on it, and started. ¶
after: ¶ Mrs. Kowalski had Pickering here at nine, same as she said. That put Havemeyer here at ten, by her count.
target: “Eight o’clock, Colquitt. Nobody else. Nine, Pickering and Colquitt. Nobody else at all. Ten, Havemeyer and Colquitt. Nobody else, that hour.”

before: Midnight. The office on Mulberry Street was dark except for the desk lamp, and the street under the window had gone quiet. I gave up on bed around eleven and made my peace with the desk chair, which had never once let me sleep. The stairs outside creaked twice, some tenant getting home. ¶ I heard steps on the stairs, stopping on every landing to think it over. A woman came in, coat buttoned against the cold, and asked straight off what it would cost. I liked her. ¶ “It’s Duchess,” Coffin said. “My Pomeranian. She’s gone from her cushion by the radiator.” ¶ I offered her the chair, and dusted it first, which I don’t do for everybody. ¶ “I had people in at eight,” she said, “for a birthday supper. Cheatham and Petrosino. Nobody else came.” ¶ “Sirkin lodges with me, and her key is lost again,” my client said, “so I left the door unlocked.” ¶
after: ¶ She had it worked out, the way people do when they can’t sleep. “The terrier next door went off at ten o’clock, the way it does when somebody’s on the stairs.”
target: “When did this happen, as near as you can say?”

before: It was a long walk from there to the Coffin flat, uptown and east, with my collar up. A cat on a step watched me go by and decided I was nobody’s business, which is the most a cat will do for you. ¶ The Coffin parlor floor on Stuyvesant Street was two tall rooms with folding doors between them, a thick carpet and a smell of beeswax. A framed sampler on the wall said Bless This House in red cross-stitch. ¶ Coffin showed me in and stood by the place where Duchess belonged, holding Duchess’s dish as if it might be wanted any minute. ¶
after: ¶ If she went at ten, she went after the supper, and everybody at the supper had known the way in.
target: Nobody minded who came and went.

before: I asked Coffin to wait in the hall, and went over the parlor by myself. ¶ She told me twice where everything usually was. I let her. It was her flat, and it was the only thing she could do. ¶ The cushion by the radiator was empty. The door was still unlocked, and there wasn’t a mark on it. Whoever it was had walked straight in. ¶ So whoever it was knew the way in, and the people who knew were the ones at the supper in the Coffin flat at eight. Coffin had given me their names. ¶
after: ¶ I read the sampler again. It was asking a lot.
target: Sirkin’s evening was still a blank in my notebook, and she was at Mrs. Nagy’s.

before: Mrs. Nagy’s was a couple of blocks downtown and east, and I took it at a good clip. A lit window hung in the fog above me with nothing holding it up. ¶ Mrs. Nagy’s, on East Fourth Street, was quiet at this hour. The hall smelled of paprika and floor wax, and a lamp had been left on at the turn of the stair. The stair had a brass rod on every step, and one of them was loose. ¶ Mrs. Nagy sat in the open door of the front room with a basket of mending, where the stair was never out of sight. She had a big ring of keys at her waist and reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and looked at my shoes before my face, to see what they’d do to the stairs. Sirkin was at the window with the curtain held back an inch, keeping an eye on the street. ¶
after: ¶ I took it all in, which didn’t take long, and then took it in again.
target: A landlady who sits on her stairs knows who used them.

before: I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Sirkin. ¶ I got as near to her as manners allowed and said my name. Young and tidy and a little tired, she still had the mark of the headset band pressed into her hair. I asked her for her evening, in order, the way you’d ask for a receipt. ¶
after: ¶ “I was home at Mrs. Nagy’s from eight through ten. At eight it was just me; Petrosino was there at nine; at ten it was just me. Eleven o’clock I went in to the print shop to set type for the morning, by myself.”
target: She asked why I wanted to know, and then told me before I could answer.

before: I headed downtown and west for the print shop, a long walk away. The cat from the step was on a different step now. Even the cat had somewhere to be. ¶ I went in at the print shop on Centre Street, which runs a night shift. The presses were running with a noise like a train going over a long bridge, and everything in the room smelled of ink and hot oil. A wooden chair with one short leg stood by the wall, and rocked whenever anything touched it. ¶
after: ¶ Whoever runs the floor at night keeps the book of who came on and who went off.
target: Callahan was at a desk on a raised step at the end of the room, where she could see everybody and everybody could see her seeing them.

before: Callahan saw me coming before I’d decided to come. That’s the job. ¶ I asked her to take me through the night, hour by hour, everybody in the place. She went through it the way you’d count change, carefully and out loud. ¶ “Two union men I didn’t know were there the whole time I was on. Ten and eleven, Sirkin. I came on at ten. Before that I couldn’t tell you.” ¶
after: ¶ I didn’t sit in the chair with the short leg. I was unsteady enough.
target: Sirkin said home at ten. The foreman had her here at ten o’clock. They couldn’t both be true, and Callahan had no reason to be the wrong one.

before: The Orpheum lay a few blocks east. A policeman on his round tried a shop door, found it locked, and looked almost disappointed. ¶
after: ¶ Mulcahy stood at the back of the house with a flashlight, pointed at the floor, ready. She had a roll of tickets on a spindle and a coin changer on her belt, and a callus on one thumb from tearing stubs, the only part of the job that showed. Cheatham was sitting near the front, very upright, with both hands on the back of the seat in front. Weisglass stood at the back with her hat in her hand, as if she had just come in or was just going. Petrosino sat in the back row with her hat on her knee, watching the picture without looking at it.
target: I went in at the Orpheum, a picture house with continuous shows till midnight. The last show had let out, the screen was a big gray blank, and the rows were full of peanut shells and dropped programs. Above the lobby doors a painted plaster mask grinned down at everybody who came in, with the tip of its nose missing.

before: I sat down in the row behind Cheatham and leaned forward, like a man with a question about the seats. ¶ I asked Cheatham to tell me her evening, from the beginning, and not to leave out the dull parts. She told it the way you give somebody directions, landmark by landmark. ¶
after: ¶ So the Coffin flat at eight, with Petrosino, which was what Coffin had said. So far as it went, it stood up. For ten, the hour that mattered, she said the Orpheum. I didn’t believe it or disbelieve it. I wrote it down.
target: “I was at Coffin’s at eight, for the supper, with Petrosino. Come nine, I left the supper to get some air and had a ticket for the Orpheum, and stayed the rest of the evening. Weisglass was there at nine; at ten it was just me; Weisglass and Petrosino were there at eleven.”

before: I asked Mulcahy for a minute, and she gave me one, and kept an eye on the room the whole of it. I asked her to count the night for me, face by face. ¶ She answered at once. It was all there, the way it always is with somebody whose job is to notice. ¶ “Pardo was there all evening, every hour of it. He buys things. Eight o’clock, Weisglass. Nobody else. Nine, Cheatham and Weisglass. Nobody else at all. Ten, Weisglass and Petrosino. Nobody else, that hour. Eleven, Cheatham, Weisglass and Petrosino. Nobody else.” ¶
after: ¶ The thumb with the callus was twitching for a stub. I didn’t have one. I rarely have a ticket for anything.
target: Cheatham said the Orpheum at ten. Mulcahy had Weisglass, Petrosino and Pardo here at ten o’clock, and nobody else. Two stories about her at the same hour, and only one of them could stand.

before: Cheatham had told me the Orpheum at ten, and Mulcahy’s list said otherwise. It was time she heard about the other one. I found her page in my notebook and kept my thumb in it. ¶
after: ¶ Cheatham looked hurt, the way people do when the world won’t agree to their version of it. “All right. I took it. It’s with Pardo, a man who buys things and asks nothing. I lost my job on Friday.”
target: “Let me read you something back,” I said. “You told me the Orpheum at ten. Mulcahy had Weisglass, Petrosino and Pardo at the Orpheum at ten o’clock, and nobody else.”

before: Midnight. My office was a room at the top of the stairs on Mulberry Street, with a desk, a lamp and a coat stand that had outlasted two tenants. Money sat in the office for once instead of a promise of it. I lit a cigarette slowly, like a man with a bank account. The cold stayed outside the glass where it belonged. ¶ Feet on the stairs, four flights of them, taken slowly. Nobody climbs four flights at midnight for the view. A man stood in the doorway, cap on, deciding if I was worth coming in for. Narrowly. ¶ “Augustus Colquitt,” he said, and put his hat on my desk like a deposit. “I was Meyer Rosenbaum’s business partner, until tonight, and I don’t like how tonight went.” ¶ Rosenbaum was a pawnbroker. At half past eleven, Bledsoe, who heard his radio still going and knocked, found the body in his own two rooms over the bakery on Hester Street. The police had a look and called it his heart. ¶ I offered my client the chair and turned the lamp away from him. ¶ “Do they know when?” ¶ “Here’s what they don’t want to hear,” he said. “His mantel clock was knocked over and stopped at five past, but it was never right: nine or ten o’clock, I’d say.” ¶ “Every night it was Hanley’s, earlier on,” he said. “Tonight too. The usual.” ¶ “Who had a reason?” ¶
after: ¶ Colquitt put fifty dollars on the desk in tens, squared the edges and pushed them across. “I want a name. The right one.”
target: “If you want a name, it’s Salerno,” he said. “He closed his business.”

before: Rosenbaum’s place was only round the corner, and I was there before I’d finished a thought. The cold had come down with the dark and meant to stay, and people were walking fast with their collars up and their opinions to themselves. ¶ I went up to Rosenbaum’s two rooms over the bakery on Hester Street. Two rooms, a front and a back, with the police gone and the clock on the shelf still ticking, as if nobody had told it. A radiator under the window knocked every so often, as if it wanted to be let in on something. ¶ Rosenbaum was still where they’d found the body, in the chair by the table, as if waiting for something that had come. ¶ Colquitt, my client, was already there, keeping one eye on the door and the other on me. ¶ Nobody kept a list of who came and went, on paper or in their head. ¶
after: ¶ I stood in the doorway a while before I went in. Rooms like that don’t like to be rushed.
target: If it happened at nine or ten, it happened in this room, and he’d let whoever did it in.

before: I went over the table. ¶ Colquitt didn’t come in. I didn’t ask him to. ¶ There were two glasses on the table. One smelled of rye and nothing else. The other smelled of rye and something sweet and chemical, like a hospital left out in the sun. Under the table, where it had rolled, was an empty brown bottle with a paper label from Mrs. Nagy’s. The lodgers there keep it on the hall shelf. Rosenbaum had been drinking with a friend, or with somebody who passed for one. ¶
after: ¶ I hadn’t been through the papers at Rosenbaum’s place yet, and papers go on talking after the one who kept them has stopped.
target: So the chloral came from Mrs. Nagy’s, and chloral takes twenty minutes to an hour to do its work. Whoever brought it to Rosenbaum had been at Mrs. Nagy’s earlier, to get it.

before: A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him, and I wanted to read them properly. I went through the papers with the lamp pulled close, the way you read a will you aren’t in. ¶ There was a page in there for everybody with a grudge, in a careful hand. Every one of them had a reason, and every reason was written down. ¶ Ellery: the lease on a shop, the rent owing, and a carbon of his letter calling it in. Whitfield: a court transcript, his own testimony against his brother. Salerno: the order that closed his business, with his signature on it. Bledsoe: one line, where he was in 1921, and an address. ¶ Everybody in Rosenbaum’s box had a reason. Fewer of them had been at Mrs. Nagy’s to get the chloral. ¶
after: ¶ The radiator knocked again. I didn’t answer it.
target: The one to ask was the bartender at Hanley’s, who’d been there all night.

before: I headed uptown and east for Hanley’s, a fair few blocks away. A cat on a step watched me go by and decided I was nobody’s business, which is the most a cat will do for you. ¶ I went in at Hanley’s, a saloon with sawdust on the floor. It was an old high room with a tin ceiling and a long mahogany bar, and the sawdust on the floor had collected the whole day in it: ash, peanut shells and bottle caps. A brass spittoon stood at the foot of the bar, polished brighter than anything else in the room. ¶ Mosley was polishing a glass that was already clean, which is what bartenders do instead of watching you. She had a pleasant, forgettable face, which in that trade is the whole trick, and eyes that went to the door every time it opened, and came back. Bledsoe was at the far end of the bar, reading the racing page and making little marks beside the horses. Whitfield was standing at the bar with his coat over his arm, drinking something brown in small careful sips. Ellery was on a stool with her hat pushed back, turning a coin over and over on the bar. ¶
after: ¶ I found somewhere to stand that wasn’t in anybody’s way.
target: A bartender who stands behind a bar all night knows who drank at it.

before: I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Mosley. I put a coin on the bar so she would have a reason to come over. She came over and left the coin where it was. ¶ I asked Mosley for everybody she’d seen tonight, in order, and nobody left out because she liked them. She didn’t look at the room to answer. She didn’t need to. ¶
after: ¶ Ellery hadn’t been at Mrs. Nagy’s while it was there to take. That put Bledsoe and Ellery here at ten, by her count. Colquitt had said nine or ten. Rosenbaum was at Hanley’s at nine, alive.
target: “Seven o’clock, Salerno and Ellery. Nobody else. Eight and nine, Whitfield, Ellery and Rosenbaum. Nobody else at all. Ten, Bledsoe and Ellery. Nobody else, that hour.”

before: Whitfield had been watching me ask the others, and had had time to think about it, which isn’t always an advantage. ¶ I sat down one stool away from him, which gave him room to decide about me. He had fingertips gone flat from typing all day, and was dressed for an office in a good plain way that no office would ever notice. ¶ “Mosley has you here at eight. Now tell me the rest of it, from the beginning.” ¶ He asked why I wanted to know, and then told me before I could answer. ¶ “At seven I went round to Mrs. Nagy’s to return a borrowed umbrella, with Bledsoe. Eight o’clock I stopped in at Hanley’s to get warm, and stayed the rest of the evening. Ellery and Rosenbaum were there at eight and nine; at ten it was just me.” ¶ Whitfield said Hanley’s at ten. Mosley had Bledsoe and Ellery here at ten o’clock, and nobody else. One of them was wrong. ¶ The flat fingertips were typing on nothing, a line at a time. Nobody was dictating. ¶ I lit a cigarette I didn’t want, to give my hands something to do while my head did the rest. ¶
after: ¶ Before I did anything about it, I wanted to find out from the landlady at Mrs. Nagy’s who’d been in.
target: Here’s what I had. Colquitt had said nine or ten, and Rosenbaum was at Hanley’s at nine, alive. The chloral came from Mrs. Nagy’s, so whoever used it had been there first. Ellery hadn’t. Bledsoe was at Hanley’s at ten; Mosley said so. Whitfield had told me Hanley’s at ten, and Mosley’s list said otherwise. Ellery was at Hanley’s at nine and ten; Mosley said so. Salerno hadn’t told me where he was at nine or ten, and nobody else had either.

before: From there to Mrs. Nagy’s was a few blocks. The cat from the step was on a different step now. Even the cat had somewhere to be. ¶ Mrs. Nagy’s, on East Fourth Street, was quiet at this hour. The hall smelled of paprika and floor wax, and a lamp had been left on at the turn of the stair. A holy picture hung in the hall, with a little lamp in a red glass under it. ¶ Mrs. Nagy sat on a kitchen chair at the foot of the stairs, with a rent book in her lap and a shawl round her shoulders. She had a big ring of keys at her waist and reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and looked at my shoes before my face, to see what they’d do to the stairs. ¶
after: ¶ A clock in the hall was keeping time for nobody in particular.
target: Whitfield had said he was here at seven. That was reason enough for the walk. Nobody comes or goes in a rooming house without the landlady knowing, and Mrs. Nagy had the look of a landlady who made a point of it.

before: I waited for a gap in Mrs. Nagy’s night, and when one came I stepped into it. I asked Mrs. Nagy who’d been here tonight, and said I’d take it untidy, the way it happened. ¶
after: ¶ “Seven o’clock, Bledsoe and Whitfield. Nobody else. Eight, Salerno and Bledsoe. Nobody else at all. Nine, Bledsoe. Nobody else, that hour. Ten, nobody but me. The chloral on my hall shelf was there at seven. I didn’t look again.”
target: She seemed pleased somebody had asked. Nobody ever asks the one who sees everybody.

before: I set off downtown and west for Sokol’s back room. It was a couple of blocks. My knees had the temperature a block before any thermometer did. They’ve had more practice. ¶ I went round to the back of Sokol’s bakery on Rivington Street, where the numbers are taken. It was warm from the ovens, with sacks of flour along one wall and a table by the other where a nickel bet on a three-figure number bought you a reason to get up tomorrow. An old tin sign for a cough syrup nobody makes any more was nailed to the wall. ¶
after: ¶ Mrs. Nagy’s list had Salerno at Mrs. Nagy’s at eight. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it.
target: Salerno was on a hard chair by the wall, turning his hat round and round in his hands.

before: I found Salerno at the far end, where the light gave up, and stood where he could see me without having to want to. “Mrs. Nagy has you at Mrs. Nagy’s at eight. That’s one hour. Tell me about the others.” ¶ He told it the way you give somebody directions, landmark by landmark. ¶ “I was at Hanley’s at seven, with Ellery. Around eight I went home to change, with Bledsoe. At nine I went round to Sokol’s for coffee with Sokol. Ten o’clock I went home, because my feet hurt, on my own.” ¶
after: ¶ I read the old cough syrup sign again. Relief guaranteed. I’d have settled for less.
target: Salerno said home at ten. The landlady had nobody at Mrs. Nagy’s at ten o’clock. They couldn’t both be true, and Mrs. Nagy had no reason to be the wrong one. The rest held where I could check it: Mosley had him at Hanley’s at seven, with Ellery, same as he said.

before: Salerno had told me home at ten, and Mrs. Nagy’s list said otherwise. It was time to say so to his face. I turned back to him with my notebook open, which is never good news for anybody. ¶ “One thing,” I said to him. “You said home at ten. Mrs. Nagy had nobody at Mrs. Nagy’s at ten o’clock.” ¶ He let out a breath he’d been keeping since I sat down. “All right. I wasn’t at Mrs. Nagy’s. I was at Sokol’s, in the back, putting a nickel on a number. I swore I’d stopped. Ashby was there. Ask him.” ¶ That was a hole in Salerno’s story, all right. I wasn’t sure yet it was the one I was looking for. An owned-up story is only as good as whoever’s in it with you. If it held, he had been at Sokol’s back room at ten, not home. ¶
after: ¶ The tin sign on the wall had outlasted the company and would outlast me.
target: It turned out Ashby was in the corner, out of the light.
